title: Multiple Return Values
intro: To return several values, a Rust function returns one tuple, and the caller unpacks it.

coming_from.go: Go returns several values, but Rust returns one tuple, `(i32, i32)`, and unpacks it with `let (lo, hi) = ...`. Because it's one value, you can also keep it whole in a variable and read `pair.0` and `pair.1`, which Go refuses. A Go `(value, err)` pair is written as a `Result` in Rust, not as a tuple.
coming_from.kotlin: A tuple is like `Pair` or `Triple`, with as many slots as you write, and it is destructured the same way. The fields are `.0` and `.1` rather than `first` and `second`.
coming_from.python: Tuples work much like Python's: `(lo, hi)` to build, `let (lo, hi) = ...` to unpack, `_` to skip. The type of each slot is fixed, and you read a slot with `t.0`, not `t[0]`. A Rust tuple in a `mut` variable can change in place; a Python tuple cannot.
coming_from.typescript: `(i32, i32)` is your `[number, number]` tuple type. A Rust tuple isn't an array, though: you read `t.0` and `t.1`, you can't loop over it, and you skip a slot with `_` instead of leaving it empty.
coming_from.java: Java has no built-in tuple type, so you'd write a small `record`; Rust's `(i32, i32)` is that record without a name or a declaration. You unpack it with `let (lo, hi) = ...`, and `_` skips a value you don't need.
coming_from.csharp: `(i32, i32)` is your value tuple `(int, int)`, and `let (lo, hi) = ...` is deconstruction with `_` as the discard. The difference is that Rust tuple fields have no names: you use `.0` and `.1`, or reach for a struct.
coming_from.c: C has no tuples, so you return a small struct or write through pointers; Rust's `(i32, i32)` is like an anonymous struct you never have to declare, but its layout is not promised, so it is not a C struct. `let (lo, hi) = ...` unpacks it, and `_` ignores a field.
coming_from.cpp: `(i32, i32)` is `std::pair<int, int>` (or `std::tuple`), and `let (lo, hi) = ...` is a structured binding. `_` skips a slot without naming it, and `(a, b) = f();` assigns into existing variables, as `std::tie` does.

notes: `&[i32]` is a slice: a borrowed view of some numbers. It accepts a Vec, an array, or part of one. More in the Vectors and Borrowing lessons.
Tuples can hold mixed types: `let t: (i32, &str) = (1, "a");` then `t.0`, `t.1`.
Swapping needs no temporary variable: `(a, b) = (b, a);`.
Don't reach for a tuple to return a value plus an error, as in `(value, err)`. Rust uses `Result` for that (see Errors).

gotcha.title: Indexing a tuple like a list
gotcha.looks_fine: Where a tuple or a fixed-size group is indexed with brackets, `t[0]` is the natural way to read its first slot, and the habit comes along.
gotcha.rust_sees: A tuple's slots are fields, numbered from zero, and you reach them with a dot and a literal number: `t.0`. Square brackets are not defined for a tuple.
gotcha.why: Each slot can have its own type. A bracket index whose number is only known when the program runs would have to produce a different type for each number, and the compiler has to know the type of every expression before the program runs. `t.0` names the slot in the source, so its type is known. The compiler's `help:` shows the dot form.

go.says: Go has no tuple type. A function returns several values, and you name each one at the call, so there is nothing to index.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses too: a `Pair` has no `get` operator, so `t[0]` is an error. You write `t.first`, or destructure with `val (a, b) = t`.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:3:14: error: no 'get' operator method providing array access.
    println(t[0])
             ^^^

python.says: Python indexes a tuple with brackets, and the index can be a variable. It runs and prints 3.

typescript.says: A TypeScript tuple is an array with a fixed length and a type per slot, so `t[0]` is fine and prints 3.

java.says: Java has no built-in tuple type. A `record` has accessor methods such as `r.lo()`, and nothing to index.

csharp.says: C# refuses too (CS0021): a value tuple cannot be indexed. You write `t.Item1`, or a name you gave the slot.
csharp.error: Program.cs(2,19): error CS0021: Cannot apply indexing with [] to an expression of type '(int, int)'

c.says: C has no tuple type. A `struct` has members you reach with a dot, and an array is indexed with brackets.

cpp.says: C++ refuses too: `std::tuple` has no `operator[]`. You write `std::get<0>(t)`, and the index has to be known at compile time (Rust is stricter: a literal).
